content_voiceover: When a lab lacks specific drug-level assays for DOACs, this table tells you what routine coagulation tests can still tell you, and their limitations. For dabigatran, the thrombin time, TT, can rule out its existence entirely, if TT is normal, dabigatran is essentially excluded, because TT is extremely sensitive to even trace thrombin inhibition. To rule out an above-therapeutic level of dabigatran, you can use APTT, a normal APTT likely excludes a supratherapeutic level, though it cannot confirm a normal or subtherapeutic level precisely. For rivaroxaban and edoxaban, there is no test that can rule out the drug's existence entirely, but PT can be used to rule out an above-therapeutic level, a normal PT likely excludes toxic levels. Apixaban is the most problematic, there is no assay, neither PT nor APTT, that reliably rules out its existence or excludes a supratherapeutic level. This is a critical clinical and board point, apixaban can be present at clinically significant levels even with completely normal PT and APTT. When in doubt with apixaban, especially before urgent procedures or in bleeding patients, a drug-specific anti-Xa assay calibrated to apixaban is needed.
keypoints: TT can rule out dabigatran's existence entirely if normal
Normal APTT likely excludes supratherapeutic dabigatran
Normal PT likely excludes supratherapeutic rivaroxaban or edoxaban
Apixaban: no PT or APTT result reliably excludes clinically significant levels
keypoint_voiceover: Remember this practical algorithm. Thrombin time can rule out dabigatran's existence entirely when normal. A normal APTT likely excludes a supratherapeutic dabigatran level. A normal PT likely excludes supratherapeutic rivaroxaban or edoxaban levels. But apixaban is the exception, no PT or APTT result can reliably exclude a clinically significant level, so a calibrated anti-Xa assay is needed.
